items.stem: Explain why Perry et al. expected the effect of oxytocin to depend on empathy.
items.answer: The social salience idea suggests oxytocin makes social cues more noticeable; people with different empathy levels interpret those cues differently, so oxytocin might lead some to approach and others to keep more distance.

items.stem: Grace, a student in Dubai, feels uncomfortable when a stranger on a bus sits very close, but happily sits close to friends. Suggest how oxytocin might influence Grace’s reaction, according to Perry et al.
items.answer: It could make the social cues from the stranger more salient; depending on Grace’s empathy level, Grace might want more distance (low empathy) or show little change (high empathy).
items.markingKey: 1 mark salience; 1 mark depends on empathy [2]

items.stem: Evaluate Perry et al.’s (2015) study of personal space and oxytocin in terms of one strength and one weakness.
items.answer: Strength (controls): The study was double-blind and placebo-controlled, so neither participants nor researchers knew who had oxytocin, reducing demand characteristics and researcher bias. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Describe the procedure of Perry et al.’s study.
items.answer: Male participants completed an empathy questionnaire and attended two sessions, receiving oxytocin or a placebo nasal spray (double-blind, counterbalanced). In the CID task they imagined standing in a room as a figure approached and pressed a key to stop it when they felt uncomfortable; preferred distance was recorded.

items.stem: Describe the main results of Perry et al.’s study.
items.answer: Oxytocin changed preferred distance depending on empathy: low-empathy participants kept a larger distance after oxytocin than after placebo, especially from strangers, whereas high-empathy participants showed little or no increase.

items.stem: Evaluate Perry et al.’s (2015) study of personal space and oxytocin, including a discussion of validity of the empathy measure.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The findings suggest that oxytocin effects depend on individual empathy, which matters for possible treatments using oxytocin for social difficulties. Strength (repeated measures design): Each participant was tested with both oxytocin and placebo in counterbalanced sessions, so individual differences in personal space did not affect the comparison. Weakness (generalisability): Participants were male students, so the results may not apply to women, for whom oxytocin effects may differ, or to other age groups. Weakness (validity of the empathy measure): Empathy was measured by self-report questionnaire, which may be affected by social desirability. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the effects of hormones on social behaviour depend on individual differences? In your answer, you may refer to individual and situational explanations and biological influences on social behaviour.
items.answer: Arguments for: Perry et al. found oxytocin affected personal space differently in low- and high-empathy participants. Individual traits moderate biological effects. Arguments against: Situations (who is approaching) also changed preferred distance. The task was artificial and used only male participants. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Evaluate Perry et al.’s (2015) study of personal space and oxytocin, including a discussion of standardisation.
items.answer: Strength (controls): The study was double-blind and placebo-controlled, so neither participants nor researchers knew who had oxytocin, reducing demand characteristics and researcher bias. Strength (standardisation): The Comfortable Interpersonal Distance (CID) task was computer-based, so every participant saw the same figures approaching in the same way. Weakness (ecological validity): Pressing a key when a figure on a screen gets too close is unlike real face-to-face interaction, so personal-space preferences may differ in real life. Weakness (validity of the empathy measure): Empathy was measured by self-report questionnaire, which may be affected by social desirability. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
